meta.title: This Country Redrew the Map So It Could Share One Calendar Day
meta._convention: Duration omitted per beat -- filled from measured narration length. Kiribati (KI) is in country-codes.json but is NOT present in the world-atlas 110m countries dataset (confirmed by direct node lookup against countries-110m.json), so highlight stays [] throughout -- markers/lines carry the whole visual, per the 'scenes that aren't a country' pattern. IMPORTANT longitude convention: beats spanning the antimeridian (crossing 180 degrees) use a single CONTINUOUS longitude scale where the Line Islands' true negative longitude (e.g. -157.4) is written as +202.6 (i.e. +360) instead, for BOTH camera bbox and markers/lines within that beat, so d3.geoMercator's raw (non-wrapping) projection renders them in the correct visual position without the camera box needing west>east wraparound math. Real-world reference: Tarawa/Gilbert Islands ~172.98E,1.33N; old date line ran along 180 degrees; Kiritimati (Christmas Island) ~-157.4,1.87N (=202.6 continuous); Millennium/Caroline Island ~-150.2,-9.94 (=209.8 continuous, first land on Earth to see each new day).

beats.voText: This country spans more than a thousand miles of Pacific Ocean, so far, its own calendar used to split down the middle.
It's called Kiribati, dozens of islands stretching from the Gilbert Islands to the Line Islands, almost a third of the way around the globe.
The date line used to run straight through the country, putting its eastern islands a full calendar day behind the west.
beats.onScreenText: The date line cut it in half.

beats.voText: In 1995, Kiribati simply redrew the map, bending the date line east, around its own islands, so the whole country shared one single day.
Now its easternmost islands sit fourteen hours ahead of New York, making Kiribati the very first place on Earth to greet each new day.
beats.onScreenText: First to see each new day.

beats.voText: One country moved the actual date line just to share a calendar with itself, and now it's the first place on Earth to see tomorrow. Follow for more places on Earth that shouldn't exist, but do.
